explanations.answer: Because the LORD does not change
explanations.explanation: That's the reason He gives, friend. He says, “Because I, the LORD, do not change, you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed.” (Malachi 3:6) Jacob's descendants were not the steady ones here. God was. Think of the one oven in my bakery that never swings in temperature. That's the one you trust with the batch.

I get why you'd pick it, baker. But the very next verse says they turned away from His statutes and did not keep them (Malachi 3:7). So their record isn't what kept them standing. The LORD says it's because He does not change (Malachi 3:6). Their good behavior was not holding that whole thing up.

Hold on, friend, that one runs the wrong way. Their offerings are exactly where the LORD says they're robbing Him (Malachi 3:8). So that can't be what kept them from destruction. The reason is that He does not change (Malachi 3:6). I'd have loved to say they earned it, but the text says otherwise.

That's it, baker. After all those years, the LORD doesn't say, "Pack it up." He says, “Return to Me, and I will return to you.” (Malachi 3:7) The door is open. I know a little about being found after a long stretch in the dark, so that line hits me right in the apron.

Nope, friend, nothing in this passage sends them out of the land. What He says is, “Return to Me, and I will return to you.” (Malachi 3:7) He's calling them toward Him. Nobody gets told to go pack a bag.

Good guess if you're picturing a big fix-it project, baker. But the LORD doesn't ask for anything new to be built. He says, “Return to Me, and I will return to you.” (Malachi 3:7) The answer is coming back to Him, not starting a construction job.
True, baker! The LORD of Hosts says, “Return to Me, and I will return to you.” (Malachi 3:7) Hear that? It's an invitation with a promise riding on it. When they come back, He comes back to them.

I see why you'd hesitate, friend, because they'd been turning away for a long time. But the text says the opposite. The LORD of Hosts says, “Return to Me, and I will return to you.” (Malachi 3:7) So if they return, He returns. That's what He says, and I'm holding onto it.

Yes, baker! The text says, “But you ask, ‘How can we return?’” (Malachi 3:7) They want to know how it's done. I think that's a fair question, honestly. I've asked "how" at the oven door more times than I can count.

Close in sound, friend, but that's not the question they ask. The people say, “How can we return?” (Malachi 3:7) They're asking about their own coming back, not about when He'll show up. It's a small switch in the words that changes who's doing the returning.

That one has some attitude in it, baker, and the text doesn't give it to them. They ask, “How can we return?” (Malachi 3:7) The question is about the way back. I'd rather not put words in their mouths that aren't there.

That's it, baker. They ask, “How do we rob You?” and the answer is short: “In tithes and offerings.” (Malachi 3:8) No long speech and no hint of a riddle. The LORD tells them plainly where the problem is.

Feasts and Sabbaths are real things in Scripture, friend, but they aren't the answer here. When the people ask how they rob Him, the LORD says, “In tithes and offerings.” (Malachi 3:8) That's the exact spot He points to. It's good to keep the text's own words close.

I like the creative guess, baker, but that's not what He says. The LORD answers their question with, “In tithes and offerings.” (Malachi 3:8) Nothing about words or songs shows up in that verse. It's about what they were supposed to bring.

That's the tricky one, friend, because a few folks would be easier to hear. But the LORD says, “You are cursed with a curse, yet you—the whole nation—are still robbing Me.” (Malachi 3:9) He says the whole nation. So it's not a handful of people.

Right, baker. The LORD doesn't say a few. He says, “You are cursed with a curse, yet you—the whole nation—are still robbing Me.” (Malachi 3:9) The whole nation is in it. Nobody gets to look around and say, "Well, I'm not the one."

Yes, baker! He says, “Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house.” (Malachi 3:10) The tithe goes in so there's food in His house. As a guy who lives by the oven, I like where this is going.

Gold sounds fancy, friend, and I know a gold base when I see one. But the LORD doesn't say gold in this verse. He says the tithe goes into the storehouse “so that there may be food in My house.” (Malachi 3:10)

Peace is a lovely word, baker, but it's not the one in the verse. The LORD says to bring the full tithe into the storehouse, “so that there may be food in My house.” (Malachi 3:10) The word is food. It's a plain, practical thing to stock up on.

That's the word, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, “See if I will not open the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing without measure.” (Malachi 3:10) Without measure means no cup, no scoop and no limit. I've never had that much sprinkles in my life, and I'd still take it.

I get why your mind went there, friend, since the people were in trouble. But in this verse the LORD says He will “pour out for you blessing without measure.” (Malachi 3:10) That's the word on the table. It's good news, and it's poured out big.

Fire is a good word for a guy with ovens, baker, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says He will open the windows of heaven and “pour out for you blessing without measure.” (Malachi 3:10) What comes pouring down is blessing.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “I will rebuke the devourer for you, so that it will not destroy the fruits of your land.” (Malachi 3:11) He's the One standing between that devourer and their harvest. That's a promise worth a good cookie box.

Walls would be a fair thing to protect, friend, but they're not mentioned in this verse. The LORD says the devourer “will not destroy the fruits of your land.” (Malachi 3:11) It's about what the ground produces.

Flocks matter, baker, and the Bible talks about them a lot. But this verse names something else. The LORD says He will rebuke the devourer “so that it will not destroy the fruits of your land.” (Malachi 3:11) So the answer is the fruits of the land.
Careful, friend, this one flips it around. The LORD says the vine in their field “will not fail to produce fruit.” (Malachi 3:11) So the vine does not fail. That's the promise in the verse.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, “the vine in your field will not fail to produce fruit.” (Malachi 3:11) The vine is going to produce. A promise that big makes me want to check my own cookie boxes twice.
That's it, baker! The LORD of Hosts says, “Then all the nations will call you blessed.” (Malachi 3:12) The whole world takes notice. They'd look at Israel and say that word.

I can see why that came to mind, friend, since the people had made some rough choices. But the LORD says the nations “will call you blessed.” (Malachi 3:12) The word is blessed, and it's a big turnaround.

I'm glad that's not the answer, baker, because I know that word too well. In this verse the LORD says, “Then all the nations will call you blessed.” (Malachi 3:12) Blessed is what the nations say, so the word is blessed.
